facts.text: A bando is a catered feast held under tents, often by a road, in a temple square or at a community center, with stoves and work tables set up beside it so the food is cooked on the spot.
Bando are held for weddings, funerals, housewarming parties, birthdays, company year-end parties and temple festivals.
The master chef (zongpushi) decides the dishes and the order of events for the whole banquet.
Bando dishes come out one by one: a cold plate first, which can wait for late guests, then hot dishes such as thick soups, seafood and meat.
Common main dishes include crab with sticky rice, steamed grouper and Buddha Jumps Over the Wall; the meal often ends with hot chicken soup, then sweets and fruit.
The chef's helpers, called water feet (shui-ka), wash and cut vegetables, prepare food, carry dishes to the tables and wash the plates.
Helpers are called water feet because their work keeps them in contact with water.
In farming times, the banquet chef came to the host's home the day before the banquet to make sausages, fried meatballs and fish balls.
With no refrigerators, some food was cooked early and hung to dry under a shed, and someone had to guard it so that it was not stolen or taken by cats and dogs.
Neighbors lent tables, stools and bowls, and each family marked its name under its things so they could be returned correctly.
A home wedding banquet usually ended after about two hours.
After the banquet, leftover dishes were cooked together into a big pot of soup and shared with the neighbors who had lent things or helped.
Bando became a professional trade in the 1960s, and the 1970s and 1980s were its golden years.
Canvas tents for bando were often supplied by drink companies, so a bando tent was jokingly called the Hey Song Grand Hotel, after a soda brand.
Modern master chefs also take orders, control costs, plan menus and organize the work of their teams.
At its peak, Neimen in Kaohsiung had about 150 master chefs, and almost one in five households lived on bando work.
In 2020, COVID-19 cut many bando chefs' orders by about 90 percent.
Bando use round red tables and red plastic chairs, and the host goes from table to table to raise a toast.
For a university bando in 2025, the caterer set up an outdoor kitchen the day before and was already preparing and cooking food at about 4 a.m. on the day.
At that university bando, almost every table finished its food, and some guests took leftovers home.
At bando in southern Taiwan, fruit may be placed in the middle of the table for guests to eat between dishes.
In old Zuoying, Kaohsiung, there were once more than 30 bando master chefs, but only about a third of them remain.
A Zuoying bando had a menu of 12 dishes that included local water chestnuts.
